sources.title: Emily Wilson · The Odyssey
sources.evidence: Confirms verse translation and the Norton Critical Edition’s notes, summaries and contextual essays.
sources.limitations: Publisher/translator description, not comparative proof of superiority.

sources.title: OpenLearn · Getting started on ancient Greek
sources.evidence: Eight sessions cover reading, sounds, writing, words, endings, sentence patterns and review.
sources.limitations: Introductory taster, not an independent-reading qualification.

sources.title: OpenLearn · Getting started on classical Latin
sources.evidence: Introductory Latin learning resource.
sources.limitations: External learning content; no enrolment or marking arranged.

sources.title: Cambridge · An Independent Study Guide to Reading Greek
sources.evidence: Second-edition companion supplies translations and exercise answers for self-study.
sources.limitations: The textbook itself was not read; purchase/library access needed.

sources.title: Hackett · Familia Romana
sources.evidence: Identifies the graded Latin reader with 35 chapters.
sources.limitations: Full page access failed; bibliographic lead, not consulted textbook evidence.

sources.title: Hackett · Five Dialogues
sources.evidence: Identifies Grube translations revised by Cooper.

sources.title: Dickinson · Core Vocabulary
sources.evidence: Latin and Greek core lists with frequency basis and limits; supports vocabulary review.
sources.limitations: Corpus frequency is not proficiency certification.

sources.title: Dickinson · Allen and Greenough: Alphabet
sources.evidence: Explains Latin alphabet and editorial I/V/U conventions.
sources.limitations: Historical reference grammar, not a graded course.

sources.title: Dickinson · Aeneid 1.1–11
sources.evidence: Latin passage with commentary for guided advanced reading.
sources.limitations: Requires grammar preparation; not beginner material.

sources.title: MIT Internet Classics Archive · Iliad

sources.limitations: Older translation; index does not establish exact composition year.

sources.title: MIT Internet Classics Archive · Apology
sources.evidence: Jowett translation supports a short argument-analysis activity.
sources.limitations: Older diction; detailed citation numbering should be checked in an annotated edition.

sources.title: MIT Internet Classics Archive · Aeneid
sources.evidence: Free older English translation with book divisions.
sources.limitations: Not a substitute for modern commentary.

sources.title: Folger · Julius Caesar
sources.evidence: Act and scene organisation supports rhetorical close reading.
sources.limitations: Early modern reception, not evidence directly from republican Rome.

sources.title: Columbia · Digital Dante
sources.evidence: Existing syllabus points to parallel text and commentary.
sources.limitations: Current access denied; previous handoff description not freshly confirmed.

sources.title: The Met · Greek Art in the Archaic Period
sources.evidence: Context for Archaic art and cultural development.
sources.limitations: Broad overview; dates are approximate period conventions.

sources.title: The Met · The Roman Republic
sources.evidence: Republican institutions and traditional 509 BCE starting date.
sources.limitations: Traditional chronological boundary is distinguished from secure event evidence.

sources.title: The Met · Marble statue of a kouros
sources.evidence: Attic marble funerary figure, ca. 590–580 BCE, accession 32.11.1; public-domain image.
sources.limitations: Museum provenance and interpretive account; observation alone cannot establish social identity.

sources.title: The Met · Cubiculum from Boscoreale
sources.evidence: Fresco room dated ca. 50–40 BCE; villa buried in 79 CE.
sources.limitations: Modern museum installation must be distinguished from original domestic setting.

sources.title: Acropolis Museum · Parthenon Gallery
sources.evidence: Building programme begun 447 BCE; architectural and sculptural context.
sources.limitations: Gallery arrangement is modern; images not copied without a confirmed licence.

sources.title: The Met · Open Access
sources.evidence: Open Access permits reuse of designated public-domain images.
sources.limitations: Permission applies only to designated images, not all website material.

sources.title: Corinne Pache · Review of Emily Wilson’s Odyssey
sources.evidence: Praises readability and apparatus while questioning some diction and interpretive choices.
sources.limitations: One critic’s assessment; supports comparison, not universal superiority.

sources.title: Penguin Random House · The Landmark Herodotus
sources.evidence: Confirms Andrea L. Purvis translation, Robert B. Strassler’s editing, maps and scholarly appendices.
sources.limitations: Bibliographic and apparatus evidence; promotional superlatives are not adopted.

sources.title: Major and Laughy · Ancient Greek for Everyone
sources.evidence: A freely accessible progression through morphology and syntax.
sources.limitations: Only selected chapters inspected; no claim to have audited the entire textbook or its feedback provision.

sources.title: Ancient Greek for Everyone · Third Declension Nouns: Part I
sources.evidence: Introduces parsing nouns by gender, number and case, with paradigms and practice.
sources.limitations: Same textbook as age-open; not an independent endorsement or a complete grammar course.

sources.title: Ancient Greek for Everyone · Greek Word Order
sources.evidence: Supports practice linking noun endings and sentence roles.
sources.limitations: Same textbook as age-open; this practice does not establish fluent authentic-text reading.

sources.title: The Met · Hydria attributed to the Berlin Painter
sources.access: Museum object record and image metadata read
sources.evidence: Attic red-figure water jar, ca. 500 BCE, with Achilles and Penthesilea; accession 10.210.19.
sources.limitations: Artist attribution is qualified; the myth’s interpretation is distinct from what is visible in the image.

sources.title: Oxford University Press · Confessions, Henry Chadwick
sources.evidence: Identifies Chadwick’s translation with introduction and notes.
sources.limitations: Direct page retrieval failed. Retained as a bibliographic lead, not a checked edition recommendation.

editions.title: Odyssey · Emily Wilson
editions.format: Modern English verse · library or purchase
editions.use: Start with the Norton Library edition for reading; choose the Norton Critical Edition when you want contextual texts and critical essays alongside the translation.
editions.caveat: Pache’s independent review praises readability and notes but questions some modern diction and the narrowing of ambiguity. Compare a passage before choosing: this is a strong option, not an uncontested best translation.

editions.title: Iliad · Samuel Butler
editions.use: Useful for accessing the assigned books and comparing how prose handles an epic scene. For close study, pair it with an annotated modern translation that retains Greek line references.
editions.caveat: Older diction and prose presentation change the experience of the poem. The website’s precise composition date should not be treated as settled.

editions.title: Plato · Five Dialogues
editions.format: G. M. A. Grube, revised by John M. Cooper · library or purchase
editions.use: A compact candidate for the Socrates module; check the second-edition contents and Stephanus references against your assignment before obtaining a copy.
editions.caveat: Publisher metadata was indexed, but direct access returned 403. Bibliographic lead; this copy has not been inspected.

editions.title: Apology · Benjamin Jowett
editions.use: Use for the first read and for comparing the opening defence with a modern translation. Keep an annotated edition with Stephanus numbers nearby for precise references.
editions.caveat: The linked text does not provide the same apparatus as a classroom edition.

editions.title: Aeneid · English reading and Latin commentary
editions.format: John Dryden’s older verse translation; Dickinson Latin commentary
editions.use: Read the assigned books in English; if you have studied Latin grammar, compare 1.1–11 with Dickinson’s text and notes.
editions.caveat: Dryden is a historically distinctive English adaptation. Dickinson is language support, not a complete English translation.

editions.title: Julius Caesar · Folger edition
editions.use: Use act, scene and line references to study speeches and performance. Read Act 3, scene 2 aloud before writing the module’s response.
editions.caveat: Shakespeare is a later reception text; do not use it as a direct transcript of Roman politics.

editions.title: Divine Comedy · Digital Dante
editions.format: Online parallel-text and commentary resource from the handoff
editions.use: The existing syllabus recommends this for canto-by-canto study; if inaccessible, use an annotated library edition preserving canto and line numbers.
editions.caveat: Direct access is currently blocked to this research tool. The resource description is retained from the handoff, not freshly confirmed.

editions.title: Herodotus · The Landmark edition
editions.format: Andrea L. Purvis translation · edited by Robert B. Strassler · library or purchase
editions.use: A practical option when geography and changes of scene make the Histories difficult to follow. Use its maps and dated outline alongside the assigned selections; consult relevant appendices after your first reading.
editions.caveat: The recommendation is based on the publisher’s documented contents, not a full comparative translation audit. Do not adopt its promotional claims about the beginnings of historical writing.

editions.title: Ancient Greek for Everyone · free grammar companion
editions.format: Open textbook · Wilfred E. Major and Michael Laughy
editions.use: Use as an accessible explanation and practice reference alongside your Greek route. Begin with the earlier chapters before the noun and word-order tasks linked below.
editions.caveat: This is a supporting textbook, not a translation of the syllabus. Selected chapters have been inspected; teacher feedback is not included.

timeline.title: Archaic Greek art and Mediterranean exchange
timeline.description: Greek artists adapt techniques and motifs through contact with Egypt and the Near East. Read the early poetry alongside material evidence.

timeline.title: Traditional beginning of the Roman Republic
timeline.description: A conventional starting point for republican government. Livy’s account belongs to a much later composition context.

timeline.title: Parthenon building programme
timeline.description: Architecture, sculpture and imperial resources intersect in fifth-century Athens.

timeline.title: Boscoreale bedroom frescoes
timeline.description: Painted architectural vistas offer evidence for elite domestic space.

timeline.title: Burial of the Boscoreale villa
timeline.description: The eruption’s date differs from the earlier date of the frescoes; their museum display is a further, modern context.

timeline.title: Achilles and Penthesilea on an Attic water jar
timeline.description: The object’s production date is distinct from the legendary setting of the scene it represents.

language.title: Guided authentic verse
language.task: After sustained grammar study, identify the main clause and subordinate constructions. Make your own prose translation, then compare an English version and explain two differences.
language.level: After foundations · advanced relative to the taster
rubric: Justify grammatical choices, not just dictionary meanings.
Identify one word whose translation needs context.
List the help you still used.

language.title: Free bridge from the taster to grammar study

language.task: Use the linked noun lesson to build a parsing sheet: dictionary form, gender, number, case and likely sentence role. Attempt its exercises before consulting aids. Record two mistakes and explain the corrections.
language.level: After the introduction · optional free route
rubric: Distinguish grammatical gender from the identity of a person.
Explain the role suggested by a case ending.
Record the chapter range actually studied.

language.title: Reading by endings, not English word order
language.scope: Ancient Greek for Everyone, chapter 8: Greek Word Order.
language.task: Read the chapter examples. For three sentences, identify the verb and justify the subject and object from their forms. Explain how changing English word order differs from changing the order of the Greek words.
language.level: Guided sentence reading · after noun foundations
rubric: Cite the example studied rather than inventing a grammatical rule from memory.
Use morphology and context together.
List any ambiguous forms that need more context.

exercises.title: A defence against eloquence
exercises.scope: Plato, Apology: the opening defence, 17a–18a; use an edition with Stephanus references.
exercises.task: Reconstruct the speaker’s distinction between persuasion and truth as premises and conclusion. Give the strongest objection you can, then a reply in 300 words.
rubric: Separate a claim from its supporting reason.
Cite the passage rather than treating Plato and Socrates as interchangeable.
Address an objection that would matter if true.

exercises.title: An epic opening in two languages
exercises.scope: Aeneid 1.1–11. Translation route: compare two English versions available to you. Latin route: use Dickinson after grammar preparation.
exercises.task: Compare three consequential wording or rhythm choices. Explain what each version foregrounds. If you cannot read Latin, frame your conclusions as a comparison of English versions.
rubric: Credit both translators.
Use matched passages and distinguish wording from interpretation.
State your language-access limits.

exercises.title: Two funeral speeches
exercises.scope: Julius Caesar, Act 3, scene 2: Brutus’s and Antony’s speeches.
exercises.task: Read each aloud. Annotate a claim, an appeal to credibility and an emotional appeal. Write 400 words explaining how an imagined audience is addressed.
rubric: Identify concrete verbal or dramatic choices.
Discuss performance as well as content.
Treat this as Shakespearean reception, not a verbatim Roman record.

exercises.title: How a translator interprets Penelope
exercises.scope: The three versions of the Odyssey Book 18 passage compared in Pache’s review: Wilson 18.160–167, Lombardo 18.167–175 and Fagles 18.181–188, as cited by the reviewer.
exercises.task: Read the brief parallel excerpts on the review page. Choose two wording or syntax decisions and explain how they affect Penelope’s agency or the reader’s view of her. In 300 words, distinguish the reviewer’s argument from your own response.
rubric: Credit the translators; their printed line numbers differ.
Use short references or paraphrase rather than copying long excerpts.
Do not claim to judge fidelity to Greek if you only read the English.

exercises.title: Following a historian through a map
exercises.scope: Your existing Herodotus assignment, Book 1.1–94 (Croesus), with the Landmark maps or another labelled historical atlas.
exercises.task: Choose three places mentioned in the reading. Record each place, its textual reference and the map used. Then write 250 words explaining one claim that the geographical setting helps you understand and one that a map cannot verify.
rubric: Distinguish modern editorial maps from ancient testimony.
Keep place identification separate from evidence that an event occurred.
Identify the atlas/edition and one remaining uncertainty.

gallery.title: A kouros: body, pattern and remembrance
gallery.credit: The Metropolitan Museum of Art · Fletcher Fund, 1932 · 32.11.1 · Public domain (CC0)
gallery.context: A funerary figure whose pose draws on Egyptian models. Its modern museum setting differs from its original commemorative use.
gallery.task: Describe three visible features before interpreting them. Compare symmetry and the forward foot. What evidence would you need to identify the person or the original audience?
rubric: Separate direct observation from the museum’s interpretation.
Name the object, approximate date and material.
State one limit to what the image can establish.

gallery.title: A Roman room: painted space and status
gallery.credit: The Metropolitan Museum of Art · Rogers Fund, 1903 · 03.14.13a–g · Public domain (CC0)
gallery.context: Bedroom decoration from the Villa of P. Fannius Synistor at Boscoreale. Painted architecture extends the apparent space.
gallery.task: Sketch the principal sight lines. Identify what is a real surface and what is an illusion. Explain what a reconstructed museum room can and cannot tell us about daily use.
rubric: Refer to two visible details.
Distinguish painting date, burial date and museum installation.
Avoid treating an elite villa as representative of all Roman households.

gallery.title: The Parthenon: architecture, cult and power
gallery.credit: View images and gallery layout on the Acropolis Museum website.
gallery.context: Study a building and the later arrangement of its surviving sculpture. The museum’s gallery evokes the temple’s dimensions and orientation.
gallery.task: Open the museum gallery. Locate the cella and the main entrance in its explanation. Write 250 words connecting spatial arrangement, religious function and political resources; distinguish the ancient building from its modern presentation.
rubric: Use the museum’s description with an explicit citation.
Identify a difference between the ancient temple and the gallery.
Separate material evidence from political interpretation.

gallery.title: Achilles beyond the Iliad: myth on a water jar
gallery.culture: Greek, Attic · attributed to the Berlin Painter
gallery.credit: The Metropolitan Museum of Art · Rogers Fund, 1910 · 10.210.19 · Public domain (CC0)
gallery.context: The museum identifies Achilles and Penthesilea. The scene belongs to the wider Trojan mythic tradition; it should not be assumed to illustrate an episode in the Iliad.
gallery.task: First describe the pose, scale and placement of the figures on the vessel. Then read the museum’s identification. In 250 words, separate visible evidence, curatorial identification and narrative interpretation. What does the shape of the jar contribute?
rubric: Keep “attributed to” in the artist credit.
Do not infer an exact literary source from a shared mythic character.
Distinguish a mythic scene from a record of historical warfare.
